business.lede: You asked whether your model is competitive, smart and attractive enough for clients to sign with us over another agency, what each package should include, project prices and how to show prices. A first draft was then read twice more by us: once as a buyer comparing four firms would read it, once as an operator and a lawyer would. Neither was a real buyer or lawyer. This is the revised version.
short: Your prices fit the market, and six months is a normal minimum for firms like Kelwin. Keep the packages, the term, the pilot and a revenue share.
In the pilot: 65% of the retainer, plus $250 for each held first meeting with a buyer who fits, capped at three full months.
Drop the per-lead fee after month 3. One 3% revenue share. An exit at day 90, on written targets.
Projects at fixed fees; $3,500 a month becomes upkeep. Prices stay off the site, and are said on the first call.
business.trust_head: Figures as reported, to be re-checked before you quote them.
business.trust: We could read only search-engine summaries of each source, not the pages themselves, so every outside figure is “as reported” until checked. The main comparison, RevPartners' prices, may date from about 2022. Legal points need a US lawyer's read.
business.buyer: In that buyer's-eye read, six months as first written was a no; the pilot with these changes was a yes.
levers: The pilot fee
About 45% of the retainer
65% of the retainer
The pilot is the costliest quarter to run (about 45–70 hours a month on Launch). At 45% the fee jumps 2.2× at month 4, just when the client decides whether to stay.
During the pilot
$200–300 for each qualified lead
$250 for each held first meeting our outreach created, capped over the quarter
A “lead” invites arguments about what counts. A held meeting with a buyer who fits is easy to check, and the cap keeps the pilot under full price.
After month 3
$150 for each lead
The full retainer, with no per-lead or meeting fee
Its purpose, making up for the pilot discount, ends at month 4. It turns an “$8,000 package” into $10,100–10,700, and it reads like an appointment-setting agency.
The revenue share
4% in the pilot, then 3%, capped at $50,000 or $100,000
One rate of 3% on a signed list of companies, capped at half of six months' fees, never above $50,000 on Launch and Growth, or $100,000 on Scaling
The two rates differ by about $540 on a typical Launch client. A list both sides sign ends arguments about credit.
An exit after the pilot
Undecided; on good faith
At day 90, judged on written targets. Leaving for any other reason costs at most the discount already given
Buyer guides tell buyers to demand a 60–90-day exit. A written test can be enforced; “good faith” can't.
Projects
From $3,500–4,000 a month
Fixed fees of $6,000–25,000; $3,500 a month becomes upkeep
Buyers compare projects by fixed fee. $3,500 a month would undercut work that sells for $10–30k.
Prices on the site
Kept off the site
Kept off the site; the starting price given on the first call
The buyer hears the starting price before giving ten days to the audit, and no low number sits on a page.

includes: Positioning and messages written down for one market and its three listeners: the champion, the person who signs and the skeptic. Two or three angles tested in the pilot.
Up to 500 target accounts chosen from the deals you've won and ranked in your CRM, with up to 3 buying signals.
Email and LinkedIn campaigns we write and run, from domains and inboxes bought in your name. LinkedIn from one profile, with its owner's written yes.
Replies routed to the right person, and one or two automatic follow-ups when a buying signal appears. Up to 3 campaigns live at once.
A live dashboard and a written note every week; written readouts in week 11 and month 6.
Named add-ons up to $12,000 a month: a second market (about +$2,000), a second LinkedIn sender (+$1,000), calling (+$2,000), a second language (+$2,000).
Tools bought in your name and paid by you: typically a few hundred to about $2,500 a month.

packages.team: An engagement lead from the founding team (about 15–20 hours a month), with a Systems Engineer and a Narrative Architect as contractors: about 45–70 hours a month in the pilot, 35–50 after. One pilot at a time until a Systems Engineer is under contract.

pilot.say: Months 1–3: 65% of the monthly fee, plus $250 for each held meeting, and never more than three months at the full fee.
pilot.say_note: How to say it to a buyer.

levers_detail.title: The meeting fee
levers_detail.text: $250 for each held meeting, in months 1 to 3 only. The total over the quarter is capped at 105% of one month's retainer ($8,400 on Launch at $8,000, about 33 meetings), so the pilot never costs more than three full months. A monthly cap would give us a reason to push meetings into the next month.

levers_detail.title: What counts as a held meeting
levers_detail.text: A first meeting the buyer attended, with someone at a company that matches your written customer profile, where our outreach made the first contact. Your own inbound requests are logged and never billed. You can reject a meeting within 5 working days, for one of five stated reasons, and a list of companies you already know is signed at kickoff and never counts.

levers_detail.title: After month 3
levers_detail.text: The full retainer, with no per-lead or meeting fee. If you want the $2,000–3,000 a month the $150 fee would have brought, set the retainer higher inside your own band, for example Launch at $10,000: one number to budget, and no per-meeting invoice.

levers_detail.title: The revenue share
levers_detail.text: One rate, 3%, on companies on the list of meetings we sourced, signed by both sides, for first contracts they sign by the end of month 18. It counts first-year contract value, and is capped at half of six months' fees (Launch at $8,000: $24,000), never above $50,000 on Launch and Growth, or $100,000 on Scaling. Renewals are retainer only. On a typical Launch client it adds about 15% to six months of fees: a bonus, never payroll.

levers_detail.title: The deposit and billing
levers_detail.text: Month 1's fee plus a deposit of one month's retainer at signing ($13,200 on Launch at $8,000), applied to month 6. One invoice a month by bank transfer, due on the 1st. Kickoff waits for payment, so contractors are never paid before the client pays.

levers_detail.title: Renewal
levers_detail.text: No automatic renewal into a new fixed term. Renewal is proposed at month 5. If nothing new is signed by the end of month 6, it runs month to month at list price, with 30 days' notice either side. Or renew for 6 months at list price, 12 months at 10% off, or 24 months at 15% off with a stated 5% rise in year 2.

exit.recommendation: Offer an exit at day 90, judged on written targets. Anyone who leaves for another reason pays back the pilot discount, never more than full price.
terms: The written pilot readout in week 11 opens a window of 5 working days, which closes before month 4 is invoiced.

In that window the client may end the contract at the end of month 3, with no exit fee, if Kelwin missed a written pilot target (a deliverable, or the meetings minimum adjusted for any client delays), or if Kelwin says in writing it can't deliver. That is your “things we discover we can't fulfill” case.
Leaving for any other reason costs the pilot discount back: on Launch at $8,000, $4,400 in the typical case and $8,400 at most. It never takes the pilot above three full months.
Kelwin has the matching right if the client didn't provide access, data, purchases or approvals.
However the client leaves, everything built stays in its own accounts.
exit.why: Buyer guides tell buyers to demand a 60–90-day exit; in our buyer's-eye read, it is what made six months acceptable.
exit.if_not: If you'd rather offer no exit, call months 1 to 3 “the testing quarter”, and expect buyers to push the pilot fee back toward 45–50%.

showing.text: Three ways to handle prices, one recommended.

options.name: No numbers on the site; the starting price on the first call
options.text: The booking confirmation, or the first five minutes of the first call, says: “Engagements start at $8,000 a month on a six-month term, and the first three months cost less. Single projects start at about $6,000.”
options.for: The buyer hears the starting price before giving ten days to the audit, and no low number sits on a page.
options.against: Many buyers want prices on the page, and the starting price will travel in forwarded emails.

options.name: A starting price and a term per package, on the site
options.text: “Launch · from $8,000 a month · 6 months, the first 3 a pilot.” Growth from $15,000, Scaling from $25,000, projects from $6,000.
options.for: The market's usual shorthand. It turns away buyers below $8,000 before they use up a free audit.
options.against: It invites side-by-side comparison, and a published price is hard to raise before any proof exists.

options.name: The full rate card
options.text: Every range, the pilot percentage, the meeting fee, the revenue share and every project's price.
options.for: Fully open: buyers judge their own fit and see that the risk-sharing is fair.
options.against: It reads as a pay-per-meeting agency, and the pilot price becomes the headline.

lifecycle.text: You picked “two ways in, one spine” only because nothing else fitted. It is now two ways in, one proposal and one contract shape.

ways.name: Audit, then a package
steps: The three questions on the audit page, plus a proposed fourth about size, with no money in it. Buyers below Launch are sent to Projects, not to “not a fit”.
A booking confirmation: what to expect, a one-page NDA, and what data the audit reads.
The first call, 30 minutes: fit, and the starting price in the first five minutes.
The System Audit: free, ten working days, read-only access.
The readout call, 60 minutes, presented on the call. Proposed: send the written readout afterwards, whether or not they sign.
The proposal call: “What's fair about this” on page one, the package the readout points to plus one step down, the team by role and hours, and the fee schedule.
Signing: month 1's fee and the deposit. Kickoff waits for payment.
Kickoff in week 1: access, the written customer profile, the list of companies that don't count, and domains and inboxes bought in the client's name.
The pilot, months 1 to 3: the build in weeks 1–4, the test in weeks 5–10, the written pilot readout in week 11, then the exit window.
The full run, months 4 to 6: more behind what won, a monthly review, renewal proposed at month 5, the month-6 readout.
After month 6: renew for 6, 12 or 24 months, step up or down, or run month to month.
Handover only when the client asks: the notice month is the handover month, at no extra fee.

ways.name: A project, then a package
steps: “Ask for this project” opens Contact with the project named; a reply within two working days.
A 30-minute call decides between the project and the audit. If more than one part is breaking, it's the audit. Project prices are said here.
A written scope: the fixed fee, a typical length, what is in and out.
Payment: 20% on signing, 50% at the written go, 30% at handover.
Week one, then a written go or stop. A stop costs week one only.
The build, through to handover, with a check 30 days later.
Then upkeep from $3,500 a month, or the audit and a package (with part of the fee credited), or done.

Contractors on 30 days' notice, with a named backup for each role, before pilot dates are set.

artifacts.lede: You said the inside pages look bland and asked for drawings that hold attention, with a few wow moments. We wrote one set of rules for every drawing, then built the first three and filmed them: real-time recordings of working prototypes, with no sound.
artifacts.rules_title: The twelve rules every drawing follows
rules: Each drawing shows one real thing we do, with the real objects: a domain, an inbox, a CRM record, a quarter on a calendar. No funnels, rockets or brains.
It plays in the order things happen, three to six steps, and settles in four to seven seconds. It plays once.
Thin lines for everything, one solid part for the thing that matters, and red for at most one thing on screen.
Parts are named on the drawing in plain words, up to six labels.
A ten-year-old can follow it. One plain sentence beside it carries the idea.
The last frame explains everything, even with motion turned off or in a screenshot.
Anything that isn't a real Kelwin fact is marked once: illustrative, specimen or worked example. Never an invented client, office, person or result.
One wow per page at most, and it goes to the page's main idea.
Each drawing is redrawn for the phone, not shrunk.
Where there's something to explore, the reader can press it, and the drawing stops playing on its own.
Kelwin's own drawing language: rulers, measured lines, paper only for paper documents. No app windows, glow, icons, 3D or bounce.
Each drawing waits until it's on screen, and never plays twice.

items.title: How we build it
items.asked: You said “Order of work” should be several small sections with animated artifacts, “so it looks more proprietary than just a whole bunch of text slapped into one place.”
items.explains: “Order of work” becomes four small drawings, one per part of the build: new sending addresses warming up (one gets paused for complaints), 1,200 companies sorted down to the 38 worth a message, the written rules checked one by one until one fires, and every email and call landing on one company's record.
items.wow: The routing rules: an event runs down the ladder of rules, each one that doesn't match gets a “No”, the match closes a red block, and the next thing goes out as a drawn object (a one-page summary, or an address paused). Press any of the three events.
items.label: The numbers in the drawings are illustrative, and marked so.

films.label: The four drawings
films.caption: The whole run at desktop width: the sending setup, data and signals, the routing rules and the CRM record, each playing as it reaches you.

films.label: The routing rules, up close

turn.lede: You said today's turn looks very much like Palantir's. Here it is beside two of our own, each filmed in real time on the same click: from the homepage's red “Request a System Audit” into the System Audit page.

options.name: Today's turn
options.text: A graphite panel with a slanted edge slides across, the mark flickers on piece by piece, and the panel lifts off the next page.

options.name: Variant A: On the line
options.text: Two flat panels close, a red line is ruled along where they meet, and the Kelwin logo rises out of the line at full size, as in your footer. On the next page the logo sinks back, the panels part, and the line travels onto the short red rule under the headline.

options.name: Variant B: The ruled edge
options.text: No panel and no logo: one flat sheet with a red line along its top slides up over the page. On the next page it slides down, and the page catches the line as its headline rule.

decide.title: Which page turn do you want?
decide.text: It plays on every page change, and never for anyone whose device asks for less motion. We recommend A as the most clearly Kelwin's own: it uses your footer's logo on the line, and the line becomes the page's red rule. With A or B, the short red line under each headline is already in place when the headline writes itself in.

decide.title: Approve the drawing rules and the three drawings?
decide.text: Approve means every interior drawing follows the twelve rules, at most one wow a page, and the three drawings are built into their pages as shown. A note on one drawing goes in the box beside it.

voice.lede: You said the copy still reads as AI-made, which a strategic partner can't afford. We wrote a voice guide for everyone who writes for the site, rewrote Narrative Systems in it, then read it again ourselves as a skeptical buyer would.
short: Say who does what to what. “We set up your sending domains” beats “Domains, aligned.”
Name real things: the deck, the CRM field, the first email, the 30-minute call.
Use numbers we can stand behind, and no others.
Say each thing once, where the reader needs it.
Every section opens with a short sentence a ten-year-old could repeat.
We run what we build, every month. Everything we set up for you sits in your accounts and in your name.
voice.why_title: Why our copy read as AI-made
why: Nobody does anything, so the reader asks who does it.
37 negations, many built as “X, not Y”.
Dashes and colons doing the drama
48 long dashes, and reveals after a colon.
Metaphor in place of how it works
Loops that learn, stacks that are wired.
Handover-first lines, your name, “Kelwin, LLC” 21 times.
rules: Every claim says who does what to what.
Name the real thing you could point at.
Only numbers we've decided, sourced or labeled as an example.
Plain verbs: write, send, call, check, fix, pay, stop.
Every section opens with a short, plain sentence.
Explain a term the first time, or cut it.
Give the reason where a CFO would ask why, and nowhere else.
Say what we need, what we won't do, what happens if it doesn't work, and how to buy it.
Say the positive thing, without knocking down a false one first.
Lists only when the things are real.
Show how it works; don't reach for a metaphor.
Full sentences, except in labels, tables and buttons. No long dashes.
Short sentences, with the rhythm set by the content.
Make claims at their true size. No “genuinely”, no “every” unless it's true.
Say each thing once.
One schedule for each recurring activity, said the same way everywhere.
Every “it” and “they” points at one thing.
Retainer first: we set it up, then run it with you. Handover only when asked.
“We” is the founding team. Never a name, never “I”, never a headcount.
Proof is sourced, labeled as a specimen, or left out.
Nothing written for you appears on a live page.
The headline says what the page offers.
One point of view on each offer page that a competitor wouldn't sign.
One name, one spelling: “Kelwin”, nothing after it.
voice.rewrites_title: Ten rewrites from our pages, one shown
voice.rewrites_lede: From pages you haven't approved yet.

rewrites.before: Decide what the market hears. One version of your positioning and messaging, for every channel and seller.
rewrites.after: A pitch your buyers can repeat without you. With you, we write down what you sell, who it's for and why buyers should pick you. We test the wording in your first emails, then rewrite your website, deck and call guides around the winner. After that, we keep testing new wording every month.
rewrites.fixes: A slogan becomes the thing itself; the order (test, then rewrite) is the strategy.

rewrites.before: Your stack, wired to sell. We set up the domains, the data and the routing under your own admin. No new software to license.
rewrites.after: We set up your email, lists and CRM, and check them every week. We set up four things: your email domains, your lists of target companies, your CRM, and the rules for who gets contacted next. We work in your own accounts, and use the tools you already pay for where we can.
rewrites.fixes: The metaphor and the habit of listing three things become a counted list of real parts.

rewrites.page: GTM Infrastructure, before anything is sent
rewrites.before: Sending domains are separated and aged, SPF, DKIM and DMARC are aligned, suppression is honored, and every record is verified before anything is sent to it.
rewrites.after: Before we send a single email, we do four things. We set up separate domains for outreach, and send small amounts from them for a few weeks first, so your main domain stays safe. We fix the three settings inboxes check before they accept mail (SPF, DKIM and DMARC). We remove everyone who has opted out, and we check that every address still works.
rewrites.fixes: A sentence where nobody does anything now has “we” doing it, and the jargon is explained.

rewrites.before: The loop that learns. For teams whose pipeline report says what happened, and never why.
rewrites.after: Learn why your deals close. Every week we look at which deals moved and ask why. We call buyers from deals you've won or lost and ask what decided it. Each quarter you get a short, ranked list of what to change.
rewrites.fixes: The metaphor becomes how it works, and a ten-year-old can follow it.

rewrites.page: GTM Intelligence, what changes next quarter
rewrites.before: Quarterly calibration program. The other three answers, weighed with your leadership into one ranked list of what to build, keep and cut.
rewrites.after: What do we change next quarter? Each quarter we meet your leadership for about two hours. We bring what the weekly reviews and the buyer calls showed, and together we agree a ranked list of changes. We take off anything that didn't raise replies or meetings last quarter.
rewrites.fixes: You said this was unclear. An abstract label becomes a meeting: how long, who's there and what comes out of it.

rewrites.page: Who We Work With, the headline
rewrites.before: Real revenue, but no system under it. For companies that sell to committees, with someone inside to own what we build.
rewrites.after: For companies whose sales still depend on a few people. You already have paying customers, and several people sign off on each deal you win. But most new deals still need the founder, or one strong rep, in the room.
rewrites.fixes: An abstract “system” becomes a situation the reader recognizes; the handover test is gone.

rewrites.before: The firm behind the signature. Rameez founded Kelwin in 2026 to build revenue systems clients keep.
rewrites.after: Why Kelwin exists. Kelwin started in 2026 for B2B companies that paid an agency for a quarter of activity and ended where they started. We write their pitch, set up their email and CRM, and track why their deals close. Then we run all three with them every month.
rewrites.fixes: No name; the history and the frustration you asked for, said as who we're for. The history line is yours to confirm.

rewrites.before: Seats open as the work arrives. Remote-first and global, juniors included. Each seat is posted with its pay range when it opens.
rewrites.after: Six roles, open now. We work remotely, across time zones, and hire at every level, juniors included. Each role below shows its pay range. Apply with the form at the end of the page.
rewrites.fixes: True to your answer that all six are open; the sentence says what to do next.

rewrites.before: One piece of the system, on its own. Scoped in writing before it starts, and built to the full install's spec.
rewrites.after: One problem, fixed on its own. When a full package is more than you need, we can take on one piece, such as your email setup or your messaging. We agree the scope in writing before we start. A project can run once, or every month on a retainer.
rewrites.fixes: You said this page wasn't clear. It now says who it's for, and that a project can run on a retainer.

rewrites.before: A readout, up close. Every System Audit ends in a written document that the client keeps. We go through it together on a 60-minute call.
rewrites.after: Case reports, published with each client's yes. Each report tells one client's case, with the problem, what we did and the numbers. Ask for the full report and we'll email it to you. None is published yet, because each one needs the client's written yes.
rewrites.fixes: The page is now what you said it is: case studies, with an honest empty state.
